explanations.answer: Where He wants them to prepare it
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The disciples ask, "Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?" (Matthew 26:17). They don't just show up hungry and hope for the best. A crew that asks the question before the feast starts is a crew I'd hire.

explanations.answer: Who He wants them to invite
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, because guest lists matter. But that's not the question here. The disciples ask where He wants them to prepare the Passover (Matthew 26:17). They need an address before they can set a single table.

explanations.answer: How long the feast should last
explanations.explanation: I see the thinking, baker, but nobody asks about the clock here. The disciples come on the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread and ask where Jesus wants them to prepare the Passover (Matthew 26:17). They're after a place, not a schedule.

Yes, a house. Jesus tells them to say, "I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house." (Matthew 26:18). The meal happens under a roof, at a certain man's place in the city. Whoever that man is, he's about to get some very special company.

A field is a fun guess, baker, but that's not the place Jesus names. He says, "I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house." (Matthew 26:18). The house belongs to a certain man in the city. That's where Jesus says the Passover will be kept.

A gate is a clever guess, baker, but it's not the place Jesus names. He tells the disciples to say, "I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house." (Matthew 26:18). The word is house. And it belongs to a certain man in the city.
Not quite, baker. The text says the opposite. Right after Jesus says one of them will betray Him, "They were deeply grieved…" (Matthew 26:22). This news hit them hard.

Right, baker. Calm is the opposite of what happens. The text says, "They were deeply grieved…" (Matthew 26:22). Then they begin to ask Him one after another, "Surely not I, Lord?" I think the whole room went quiet before the questions started.

A bowl it is. Jesus says, "The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me." (Matthew 26:23). He's talking about someone sitting right there at the meal. That's what makes it so heavy.

Close on the picture, baker, but it's not a basket. Jesus says the one "…who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me…" will betray Him (Matthew 26:23). You dip into a bowl, and baskets just sit there looking handy.

A jar is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the word here. Jesus says, "The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me." (Matthew 26:23). Dipping a hand into the bowl with Him means this person is right there at the meal.

explanations.answer: What happens to Him was already in Scripture
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says the Son of Man will go "…just as it is written about Him…" (Matthew 26:24). It means what's coming was already written in Scripture. He says it right in the middle of the meal.

explanations.answer: His words will all be written down later
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, baker, but that's not what this line means. "…just as it is written about Him…" points to what Scripture already says about what will happen to Him (Matthew 26:24). It's about the path ahead, not a notebook.

explanations.answer: His name is kept in the temple records
explanations.explanation: A record book is a fun picture, baker, but the text goes somewhere else. Jesus says the Son of Man will go "…just as it is written about Him…" (Matthew 26:24). It's about what Scripture already says is coming for Him, not a name on a list.

True, and it's a heavy line. Jesus says, "…woe to that man by whom He is betrayed. It would be better for him if he had not been born." (Matthew 26:24). I think this one hurts to hear. There's no joke to make here, so I'll just let it sit.

It does sound too harsh to be true, baker, but Jesus really says it. He says, "…woe to that man by whom He is betrayed. It would be better for him if he had not been born." (Matthew 26:24). It's a heavy line. I think the room felt every word.

That's the one, baker. Judas asks, "Surely not I, Rabbi?" and Jesus answers, "You have said it yourself." (Matthew 26:25). Judas, one of the Twelve, asks a question like the ones the others asked. The answer he gets is short and plain.
Not quite, baker. Jesus doesn't tell Judas to wait. He answers, "You have said it yourself." (Matthew 26:25). It's short and it's direct.

That sounds like something a wise teacher would say, baker, but it's not what's written. Jesus answers Judas with, "You have said it yourself." (Matthew 26:25). No instructions, just those few plain words.

You got it, baker. Jesus gives the bread to the disciples and says, "Take and eat; this is My body." (Matthew 26:26). He takes it, blesses it, breaks it and hands it over. It's one of the most important moments at this table.

His word is a good guess, baker, but that's not what He says here. Jesus takes the bread, blesses it and breaks it. Then He gives it to them and says, "Take and eat; this is My body." (Matthew 26:26). The bread is tied to His body.

The kingdom does come up at this meal, baker, just a few verses later (Matthew 26:29). But when Jesus hands over the bread, He says, "Take and eat; this is My body." (Matthew 26:26). Keep an ear out for the kingdom, because it's coming.
Blood is right, baker. Jesus says, "This is My blood of the covenant…" (Matthew 26:28). He's giving them the cup and telling them what it means. Slow down and take that one in.

Yes, forgiveness. Jesus says His blood "…is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins." (Matthew 26:28). That's the heart of what He's handing them. Forgiveness for many, and the cup goes to all of them.

Word is a solid Bible word, baker, but it doesn't belong in either blank. Jesus says, "This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins." (Matthew 26:28). Blood fills the first blank, and forgiveness fills the second.
I see why you'd reach for it, baker, but judgment isn't the word Jesus uses. He says His blood is poured out "…for the forgiveness of sins." (Matthew 26:28). Forgiveness is the word in the verse.

This moment does feel heavy, baker, but "weight" isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, "This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins." (Matthew 26:28). The blanks are blood and forgiveness.

explanations.answer: Until He drinks it anew in His Father's kingdom
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus says He won't drink of the fruit of the vine "…until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father’s kingdom." (Matthew 26:29). He doesn't leave it at goodbye. He points to a day He'll drink it again with them.

explanations.answer: Until the Passover is kept again in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: A fair guess, baker, since the Passover is the whole setting. But Jesus doesn't say that. He says He'll drink it anew "…with you in My Father’s kingdom." (Matthew 26:29). The day He's pointing to is bigger than another feast.

explanations.answer: Until the Sabbath day has come and gone
explanations.explanation: The Sabbath isn't in this verse, baker. Jesus says He won't drink of it "…until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father’s kingdom." (Matthew 26:29). The day He points to is the one in His Father's kingdom.

True, baker. The text says they sang a hymn and then went out to the Mount of Olives (Matthew 26:30). After a night with that much weight in it, they still sing together. I think that's worth noticing.

It does feel like a heavy night, baker, so a hymn might surprise you. But the text says, "…when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives." (Matthew 26:30). They sing first, then they go.

Scattered is right, baker. Jesus quotes, "I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered." (Matthew 26:31). He says it's written, and He's telling them ahead of time. The sheep part is about all of them.

Gathered would be the cozy ending, baker, but it's the opposite. Jesus quotes, "I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered." (Matthew 26:31). Scattered is the word in the verse. Right after, He says that after He has risen, He will go ahead of them into Galilee (Matthew 26:32).

Sheltered sounds nice, baker, but that's not the word. Jesus quotes, "I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered." (Matthew 26:31). Scattered is what the verse says. He tells them this very night they will all fall away on account of Him.

explanations.answer: Go ahead of them into Galilee
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus says, "But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee." (Matthew 26:32). Right after the hard news, He talks about what comes after He has risen. He keeps going.

explanations.answer: Go ahead of them into Samaria
explanations.explanation: Samaria is a real place, baker, and I like that you're thinking maps. But Jesus names a different one. He says, "…after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee." (Matthew 26:32). Hold onto Galilee, and keep that map handy.

explanations.answer: Go ahead of them into Syria
explanations.explanation: Syria is a real place too, baker, and you get credit for a good guess. Still, Jesus doesn't name it. He says, "…after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee." (Matthew 26:32). Galilee is the word, so Syria can stay on the map.

Deny, baker. Jesus tells Peter, "this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." (Matthew 26:34). Peter is one of the Twelve, and he just said he'd never fall away. I think that stings.
Defend is what Peter would probably LIKE to do, baker. But Jesus says, "this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." (Matthew 26:34). Deny is the word.

Praise would be a nicer ending, baker, but that's not what Jesus says. He tells Peter, "this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." (Matthew 26:34). Peter hears it right to his face.

Peter is the one who speaks up, baker, but he isn't alone. He says, "Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You." Then the text adds, "And all the other disciples said the same thing." (Matthew 26:35). So every one of the disciples makes the promise.

Right, baker. Peter says, "Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You." and then "…all the other disciples said the same thing." (Matthew 26:35). Peter is just the one the text quotes. All of them are making big promises.
